posts.author: GrahamS
posts.content_md:
I'm interested in using holography to record images of small insects such as bees. I've seen references to holographic microscopes but from what I can tell the optics used give you a depth of field issue . What kind of resolution might I expect from a hologram at this scale?

Any general advice appreciated.

Graham

posts.author: ErichRose
posts.content_md: I recorded a mounted Honey Bee many years ago for a friend. It was shot as a split beam reflection and then copied to stand out a bit from the plate. It was possible to look at the hologram with a magnifying lense and see the small hairs and individual lenses of the eyes. The only issue was that it was hard not to cast a shadow so looking at the top of the bee was hard since the reconstruuction was from above.

posts.author: BobH
posts.content_md:
I'd think the resolution would be limited by the reconstruction source, not the optics used to magnify the insect. If you use a laser, you'll be limited because of speckle. If you use a filtered micro-short arc lamp or LED, you'll be limited by the source size and spectral bandwidth blurring.

The strong lens or lenses you use to magnify the image will distort it, but I guess you'll get pretty good results if you can accept a restricted viewing zone. Aiming good images toward one or both eyes only, like in the popular microscope or stereopticon images is another option, with a number of ways to implement. Stereogramming them is probably the best but most expensive way to go, but I think I'd like the analog approach.

posts.author: GrahamS
posts.content_md:
Thankyou ErichRose, that sounds very encouraging!

Bob, I built a interferometric microscope that used speckle to provide wide field illumination, the laser was purposefully passed through a diffuser which was then spun at high spee. Because the constantly evolving speckle was sent to both the sample and reference arm you still got interference fringes, the fact that the diffuser was spinning was averaged out by the CCD camera, the reason I did it was to allow wide field imaging but it also got rid of all that horrible unwanted interference. I wonder if something similar could be done for holography, of course vibration would be a killer. I used a brushless motor spinning a disk of laser jet film, the stuff used for printing PCB masks on to as my diffuser, that was boxed to reduce air movement.

Ideally of course I would love to create some form of high speed camera that would take say a sequence of 20 images at 4000fps, something along the lines of a photographic plate on a motor and a pulsed laser, the practicalities escape me at the moment though 

Graham

Sorry Guys, but Stereograms...SEM imagery...come on. This all seems to be taking away from the beauty and the simplicity and inherent high resolution of an, excuse me, "plain old hologram." 

I'm going to get up on my soap box for a moment here. Don't worry I will not do it very often.

My profession is Exhibit Design. Hands-on science and interactive stuff for kids and adults. I've been doing it for 25+ years. It still makes me nuts that holography is to this day considered an "expensive option" and I can recall numerous occasions when the production quote, which called for a rather simple small hologram, came back overpriced because some "holgraphic consultant" decided "oh no, what you really want is....." Same goes for lasers, especially before diodes. When I wanted a safe HeNe in the low Mws as the laser the "consultants" came back with a 5 watt water cooled argon! Jeez! they were all wacked out rock and roll show dudes who had stared into the beam one too many times. (This is a true story) These industries are still suffering from an overblown technocratic mindset that wants every project they do to either use the absolute newest equipment or push the envelope. That would be great once in a while, and the big trade show folks can afford to do it, but in my business working with mostly small non-profit children's museums and science centers those high production costs don't fly. Now don't get me wrong, I do know there are a handful of good holographers producing high quality and properly priced work, but I have had clients get get frustrated and walk away because their first encounter with the field is just so over-the-top. Oh and some of those technocrats don't have the common sense to not bad mouth each other in front of the clients and just make the industry even that much less palatable. 

I'm not trying to be a buzz kill here. But one day I would like someone to say to me "Holography, yeah, I used that on a project and it was really cool and very cost effective." (without being embossed in the tens of thousands) This is as opposed to "Yeah isn't that really complicated and expensive?" which is what I still hear to this day every time I mention them as a possibility.

I think what Graham needs is a simple, straight forward optical set up with a relatively easy operation. EX: Place prepared subject here, load film, release shutter, develop film, done. Not another 12 steps and thousands of dollars or weeks of time. If scientific journals could use holograms in place of the usual black and white plates that accompany most descriptive papers it would be truelly awesome.

I disagree here a bit Erich. The sem was just a reference to a great holo I saw that was similar to what's wanted. It was the stereogram that I was hyping in this case. If you want to see an insect, and really see the details, it needs to be magnified. Can't do that with just standard classic holos here. Not at the magnification needed. The sem was nice though as it has total depth of field.

The hologram I was talking about was the best BECAUSE of the magnification. The little microscopic bug was huge! I could see things I could never have seen on something even as large as a bee. 

Also, how could you get the little hairs on the bee's leg that holds the pollen in a "plan old hologram"to stay still? It would have to be pulsed......now its not that simple anymore. 

The orignal poster was talking about expensive microscopes so I would think he has the budget for a still camera with a macro lens. A small single axis translation stage and he's all set. All very cheap. He might even own the stuff already.

As far as the complexity of the stereogram equipment., my first setup was made in a couple of days. It was totally manual and did 36 exposures. The images that came out were pretty good. This was before boards like this existed and I was alone out here in the holo world. With the boards help and all the reference information around I'm sure it could be done a lot better than I did. To make my working table into a stereogram rig cost less than 75 bucks worth of stuff. Nowadays I would do it differently but it did work well. 

I will agree with everything you said about the quotes and all that but with some explanation. You mentioned consultants. I call them brokers and this industry is littered with them all over. People that have no experience or much knowledge. All they do is find a single production company to work with and just pretend they do it themselves. All they do is mark up. Same thing with the lasers. I think you were just running into the wrong people. Expecially in the stage industry. I've also worked with rock and roll lasers so I can relate. They just don't know anything about holography, I bet the small frame argon they suggested didn't even take an etalon. The word coherence does not exist in their industry or in most industries that use lasers for that matter. We're special

Embossed is really for high volume you must remember. Without the job being at least a few thousand small holograms its going to be expensive. That's really not than many for a real job, in fact its very small. If your talking about a local nightclub that wants a few hundred cool entrance cards that's a different story. In that case use a stock image, maybe with some custom overprinting. Now its cheap again.

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
Here is the holographic Microscopy I did and it took about 15 minutes to set up.

[http://www.holograms3d.com/PhotoGal/General/AntHolo.JPG](http://www.holograms3d.com/PhotoGal/General/AntHolo.JPG)

I took a dead ant and cut him in half. I then took an old pinhole that was clogged in the magnetic mount for a spatial filter and glued the ant on it at its abdomin and coming out of the surface. I placed the magnetic mount back in the spatial filter. I then flipped the objective around the other way in the spatial filter and was able to use the x, y, z adjustment of the spatial filter to fine tune everything. I then placed my largest lens between the ant mount and the plate to try to get the largest field of view possible.

This is pretty close to what I did.

[http://www.holograms3d.com/Illustration ... scopy3.jpg](http://www.holograms3d.com/Illustrations/HoloMicroscopy3.jpg)

While it is not an ellaborate set up and surely could have been taken to the next level (mostly a couple more object beams, it was really cool seeing the ant magnified.
